hardy

/HAR-dee/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hardy means tough enough to survive harsh or difficult conditions.

The hardy alpine wildflowers bloom right through late spring frosts that would kill most garden plants.

Example

Sled dog breeds like the Alaskan malamute are famously hardy, sleeping comfortably in the snow at temperatures that would send most pets shivering indoors.

The malamute thrives in brutal cold that other animals cannot tolerate. Surviving, and even doing well, in harsh conditions is exactly what hardy describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tough: Tough means able to endure strain, rough handling, or hardship without giving way — tough boots, a tough opponent. Hardy is more specific: hardy things ride out harsh living conditions like frost, poor soil, and bitter cold. A rope can be tough; living things and people are called hardy.

rugged: Rugged means strong and built to last, usually said of gear and equipment made for rough treatment — a rugged laptop case. Hardy points at survival rather than construction: a hardy plant or crew keeps thriving through punishing weather that would defeat most others.

sturdy: Sturdy means solidly built and not easily hurt or knocked over — a sturdy table, a sturdy fence. It is about physical build and resistance to force. Hardy is about enduring conditions: a scrawny little alpine flower can be far hardier than a sturdy-looking garden rose.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

delicate: easily damaged

frail: weak and fragile

Where it sits · how much punishment it can take

healthy → hardy → indestructible

healthy vs. hardy: A healthy plant is doing well right now, while a hardy plant keeps doing well even when conditions turn brutal.

indestructible vs. hardy: A hardy explorer endures punishing conditions, but no living thing is truly indestructible.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hard: tough, bold (from Old French hardi, made bold)

Suffix — -y: having the quality of

Put it together: The root hard carries the idea of toughness and boldness, and the suffix -y means having that quality, so something hardy has toughness built in, letting it endure conditions that defeat weaker things.

Use the root in a new word: hardship: The pioneers endured every hardship of the long journey west.

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday

Most common with plants, animals, and people who endure rough conditions, as in 'hardy perennials' or 'a hardy crew.' Do not confuse it with hearty, which means warm and enthusiastic, as in a hearty welcome or a hearty meal.
